prompt:
Extract every policy commitment stated in the text below.

Rules:
- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.
- Do not number the lines. No bullets, headings, preamble, or commentary.
- If the text states no policy commitments, output the single word NONE.

<text>
Labour’s 2010 manifesto promises a “future fair for all” built on securing economic recovery, protecting frontline services, reforming institutions, and promoting fairness and responsibility.

Economy and public finances: Labour rejects immediate 2010 cuts, prioritising recovery, then pledges to more than halve the deficit by 2014 through growth, fair tax changes and lower-priority cuts. Measures include £15bn efficiency savings, pay restraint (1% cap in 2011–13), public-sector pension reforms, asset sales, and fiscal responsibility rules. Tax changes include a 50p top rate, reduced pension relief for the highest earners, a bank bonus tax, and a 1p rise in National Insurance (shielding those under £20,000 and pensioners). VAT on essentials will not be extended.

Financial reform and growth: The manifesto backs tighter banking regulation (higher capital, living wills, global levy), competition, and support for mutuals. UK Finance for Growth will channel £4bn to SMEs and high-tech firms; a Growth Capital Fund and Innovation Investment Fund will back scaling companies. An activist industrial strategy targets one million skilled jobs by 2015 across low‑carbon, digital/creative, life sciences and professional services. Infrastructure plans include High Speed Rail, broadband for all (funded by a landline levy), a Green Investment Bank, energy grid reform, and clean energy (around 40% low‑carbon electricity by 2020 via renewables, nuclear and CCS). Corporate governance reforms will promote long-termism, higher takeover thresholds and transparency.

Jobs, welfare and living standards: The Future Jobs Fund guarantees jobs/training for young people after six months (mandatory at ten), and guaranteed work after two years’ unemployment. The minimum wage will at least match average earnings; a £40 Better Off in Work guarantee and Skills Accounts support progression. Housing measures include a two-year stamp duty holiday up to £250,000 for first-time buyers (funded by 5% rate over £1m), more affordable homes, stronger repossession protections, and council house building. A People’s Bank at the Post Office, a basic banking universal service obligation, tougher regulation of high-cost credit, and portable account numbers aim to improve consumer finance.

Education: Frontline spending on Sure Start, childcare, schools and 16–19 learning rises; more free nursery places; 3Rs and one‑to‑one tuition guarantees; personal tutors; wider parental powers to trigger leadership change; 1,000 schools in accredited groups by 2015; fair admissions and a local pupil premium. Apprenticeships expand; participation to 18 becomes compulsory; access to HE widens with funding review pending.

NHS and care: NHS spending is protected with up to £20bn efficiencies reinvested. Legally binding guarantees include 18‑week treatment waits (or funded private alternative), one‑week cancer test results, routine health checks for 40–74s, GP evening/weekend access, wider home-based care, patient choice of any qualified provider at NHS cost, and expanded mental health therapies. A National Care Service will introduce free home care for highest needs from 2011, cap residential care costs after two years from 2014, and move towards comprehensive free care after 2015.

Policing, borders and communities: Police and PCSO numbers are maintained; neighbourhood teams devote 80% of time on the beat; failing forces can be taken over. Faster, tougher anti‑social behaviour action is guaranteed. Immigration is controlled via a points‑based system (no unskilled non‑EU migration), stronger English requirements, and earned citizenship, with support for impacted communities.

Families and pensions: A new “Father’s Month” of flexible paid leave; a £4/week Toddler Tax Credit; extended flexible working and an end to default retirement at 65. The basic state pension is re‑linked to earnings from 2012; auto‑enrolment and Personal Pension Accounts expand saving.

Culture, environment and rural: The manifesto backs a “golden decade” of sport (Olympics legacy), operationally independent museums, the BBC’s independence, broadband rollout, 400,000 green jobs by 2015, pay‑as‑you‑save home insulation, a move towards zero waste, new habitat networks, maintained Green Belt, a Supermarkets Ombudsman, and support for rural services.

Democracy and devolution: Referendums on AV for Commons and a largely elected Second Chamber; fixed-term parliaments; a lobbyists’ register; potential votes at 16 after improved citizenship education; open data and digital government; stronger local government powers and city‑region devolution.

Security and foreign policy: A Strategic Defence Review, continued support to forces and veterans, maintained nuclear deterrent and multilateral disarmament, a clear Afghanistan strategy, a pro‑EU, outward-facing agenda, 0.7% aid by 2013 in law, and reform of global institutions.
